children.translated_text: Consciousness, in the form of the activity of awareness, is that which belongs to the supreme <s>Śiva</s>.

children.text: svātantryam etad evātmā tato 'sau paramaḥ śivaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This very freedom is the self; therefore he is the supreme <s>Śiva</s>.

children.text: athavā ko 'yam ātmeti praṣṭṝn bodhayituṃ śiśūn ||
children.translated_text: Or else, in order to instruct childish questioners who ask, 'What is this self?',

children.text: nātmā deho na ca prāṇo na manaḥ khaṃ na śūnyabhūḥ ||
children.translated_text: the self is not the body, nor the breath, nor the mind, nor space, nor a ground of emptiness.
Rather, the self is consciousness alone: so it has been taught by the supreme lord.

children.text: atha caitanyam evaitad ātmā svābhāvikaṃ vapuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now this consciousness alone is the self, its natural body.
Because no distinction has been enjoined, it is also the body of this universe, which is not an object of consciousness in itself.

children.text: acetyamānaṃ kasyāpi vapuḥ kim api no bhavet ||
children.translated_text: A body that is not being cognized by anyone could not be anything at all.
But what is cognized becomes consciousness-made, because it is identical with the nature of awareness.
Thus, according to the reasoning spoken by <s>Śiva</s>,
consciousness alone is the ultimate real nature of the whole universe, moving and unmoving.

children.text: nanv evaṃvidhaviśvasya caitanyaṃ ced vapus tadā ||
children.translated_text: But if consciousness is the body of a universe of this kind,

children.text: kathaṃ bandhasya sambandha iti śaṅkāṃ vyapohitum ||
children.translated_text: how can there be any relation to bondage? In order to remove this doubt,
<s>Maheśvara</s> states the sūtra by the readings with conjunction and without conjunction.
There, first, 'ignorance' means, in the self whose nature is the expansion of consciousness,
the knowledge of what is not self as self; and again, with regard to what is not self,

children.text: dehādāv ātmamānitvaṃ dvayam apy etad āṇavam ||
children.translated_text: the taking of the body and so on as 'I'. Both of these are the atomic impurity,
an impurity imagined by oneself in oneself; bondage is made manifest by one's own will.
Is this bondage simply identical with the atomic impurity? No, so it is said:
The womb, the cause of the manifestation of difference, is <s>māyā</s>; the class arisen from it
is the mass of principles from <s>kalā</s> down to earth, consisting of that.
The impurity called <s>māyīya</s> consists in the manifestation of each distinct object of knowledge.
<s>Kalā</s>, entering the body, brings limitation to human beings.

children.text: vyāpṛtiḥ puṇyapāpātmā śarīraṃ yasya tat punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Activity, whose nature is merit and demerit, has the body as its basis; that, again,

children.text: kārmaṃ ca malam etasmin dvaye bandho 'nuvartate ||
children.translated_text: is the karmic impurity; bondage continues in these two.
This triad of impurities has been stated in the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñā</s>:
The loss of the freedom of consciousness, and the unconsciousness even of freedom,
is this twofold atomic impurity, because it steals away one's own true nature.
Here the manifestation of separate objects is <s>māyīya</s>, giving birth and experience.

children.text: kartary abodhe kārmaṃ tu māyāśaktyaiva tat trayam ||
children.translated_text: But the karmic impurity belongs to the agent who lacks awareness; these three exist through the power of <s>māyā</s> alone.

children.text: ity athaiṣāṃ malānāṃ tu bandhakatvaṃ nirūpyate ||
children.translated_text: Now the capacity of these impurities to bind is explained.
That which is incomplete, having the form of otherness and consisting in the manifestation of separate objects,
whose body is the entire store of impressions from auspicious and inauspicious acts,

children.text: trividhaṃ malam uktaṃ yat tad eva jñānam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: that threefold impurity which has been described is itself called knowledge.

children.text: na so 'sti pratyayo loke yaḥ śabdānugamād ṛte ||
children.translated_text: There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words.

children.text: anuviddham iva jñānaṃ sarvaṃ śabdena gamyate ||
children.translated_text: All knowledge is understood as if pierced through by word.
According to this stated reasoning, the mother of this manifold knowledge
has as her body the fifty letters from a to kṣa.
She is the birthplace of the group of principles from <s>Śiva</s> down to earth.
Situated in the midst of the consciousness in the aperture of the skull, hanging upon the noose of <s>Brahman</s>,
the very terrible mistresses of the seats delude again and again.
Thus, according to the reasoning taught in the <s>Śrītimirodghāṭa</s>,
adorned by the circle of Mothers presiding over the classes beginning with the vowels,
'I am incomplete,' 'I am complete,' 'I am thin,' 'I am not thin':
by the penetration of words such as these, they bring about sorrow, joy, and the rest.
The basis, the presiding power, and, because of that presiding over the basis,
the cognitions of human beings, which have not obtained repose in the inward-facing self,
are constantly outward-facing and are said to be causes of bondage.
Now the means for calming the relation to bondage of this kind is stated.
It has as its true nature repose in the supreme object to be attained, according to the supreme lord.
This self-awareness, whose nature is reflective consciousness, is spreading forth;
its sudden surging-up is the rising of intuition.
The inner vibration, called exertion or upsurge, consists in the contemplation 'I am full'.
Because it is the complete harmonious union of all powers,
and because, by being filled on every side by the universe, it is capable
even of swallowing up differentiated constructs, it is, by its very meaningful name, <s>Bhairava</s>.
Now, from the attainment of <s>Bhairava</s> of this kind, since it is the cause of calming bondage,
emergence too becomes an appearance of difference that has been pacified: so it is said.
This upsurge of self-awareness that has been described, whose self is <s>Bhairava</s>,
has a great power, beyond both sequence and non-sequence.
It is eager to overrun the entire wheel of its own powers of consciousness,
and, though having the form of empty, full, and both, it is the supreme power whose nature is none of these.
By that very power, on the wall of one's own consciousness, beginning with the shining forth of objects of knowledge,
and continuing as vibration up to repose in the supreme knowing subject,
through the expansion of the powers of manifestation, maintenance, dissolution, and the nameless appearance,
the unsteady fivefold activity concerning the manifold world is unfolded.
Again, when this wheel of powers has been expanded by her,
its rejoining is the reflective contemplation of the sequence taught in the inner tradition.
When that occurs, for this universe extending as far as the level of <s>Kālāgni</s> and the other kalās,
there is dissolution, marked by the real presence of the fire of one's own self-awareness.
Thus, for the yogin whose difference has been burned by the <s>Kālāgni</s> of self-awareness,
there is said to be no distinction at all between samādhi and emergence.
In the distinction among waking, dream, and deep sleep, the experience of the fourth state arises.
The upsurge is <s>Bhairava</s>: this is the shining body whose form has been stated.

children.text: turyaṃ nāma paraṃ dhāma tadābhogaś camatkriyā
children.translated_text: The fourth is called the supreme abode, and its experience is wonder.
Even though waking and the other states are distinct, for the yogin that continuity is possible.
What remains to be taught is the interweaving whose form is supreme bliss.
The triad beginning with waking is indicated in order by three sūtras.
Waking is knowledge produced by the external senses, having an object common to all.
Dream is said to be one's own self alone; its conceptual constructs arise from oneself.
Non-discrimination, one's own non-recognition, is māyā, and delusion consists of that.
For yogins this triad, together with concentration and the rest, is deep sleep.
In the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñā</s> too, waking and the other states have been characterized.
In emptiness, whose nature is the absence of intellect and the rest, and which is the footing of I-ness and agency,
there is absence of knowable objects, consisting only of indistinct impressions of form.
The inner activity of the senses is held to impel breath and the rest.
Or, in the vital breath called life, I-ness consists of the subtle body of eight constituents.
When it remains only to that extent, it is called deep sleep, resembling dissolution.
It is joined with and separated from what is knowable and unknowable, and joined with or free from the impurity of māyā.
Even on the path of mind alone, because of the delusion that things are objects of the senses,
the vivid manifestation of entities is creation, and is regarded as the state of dream.
But that creation which, as being the field of all the senses, is stable as external,
and is common to all knowers, that is waking.
Thus, when this triad beginning with waking has been explained at length in accordance with ordinary usage,
for one who is awake with attentive awareness in this triad beginning with waking,
through the investigation of the wheel of powers, which is the cause of the withdrawal of the universe,
there flashes forth the recognition of non-difference, full of the enjoyment of the fourth state and removing non-recognition.
For the one in whom it shines without interruption, by ascending that current,
the yogin, touching the consciousness just described, becomes full of what is beyond the fourth.
The triad beginning with waking, when connected with the investigation of the aforesaid wheel of powers,
is saturated by the downpouring essence of the bliss of the fourth state, because difference has been abandoned.
Meditating on the supreme ether immersed in the essence of bliss,

children.text: tritayasyāsya yo bhoktā camatkartā sa yogirāṭ ||
children.translated_text: the one who enjoys and marvels at this triad is the king of yogins.

children.text: triṣu dhāmasu yad bhogyaṃ bhoktā yaś ca prakīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is said to be enjoyed in the three abodes, and whoever is declared to be the enjoyer,

children.text: vidyāt tad ubhayaṃ yas tu sa bhuñjāno na lipyate ||
children.translated_text: one who knows both of these, while enjoying, is not tainted.
Thus, possessing the splendor of the sovereignty of consciousness just described, without any rival,
compact with consciousness and filled with the supreme bliss of knowledge of his own self,
he is <s>Vīreśa</s>, lord of the heroes who swallow up difference,
the master of the senses as they spread within and without.
What stages are there for him, indicating ascent to and rest in the supreme conscious reality,

children.text: bhūmikāḥ santy ayaṃ yābhir yāti sarvottarāṃ sthitim ||
children.translated_text: by which he reaches the highest state of all?
To quiet this doubt in the disciple's heart, it is said at the end that such stages do exist.
Just as astonishment may arise in someone amid extraordinary bliss,
so, for this yogin, constantly, in the perception of each respective knowable object,
when his senses are stilled by the experience of incomparable supreme bliss

children.text: pare svātmany atṛptyaiva yad āścaryaṃ sa vismayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: in the supreme self, and because he is never sated, that wonder is astonishment.
That very astonishment is indeed the stage of yoga, whose form is unity with the supreme reality,
and it indicates ascent through those stages and final rest.
For the yogin whose mind has mounted the stage of yoga endowed with such astonishment,
and who, by proper reasoning, has attained eternal identity with <s>Parabhairava</s>,

children.text: tasyaiva yogino yecchā śaktiḥ saiva bhavaty umā ||
children.translated_text: that very yogin's will, his power, becomes <s>Umā</s>.
She herself is the supreme Lady, and she is proclaimed as <s>Kumārī</s>.
Through the play of creating and the rest of the universe, from <s>Sadāśiva</s> down to earth,
she is <s>Kumārī</s> also because she destroys ku, the ground of great māyā.
<s>Kumārī</s> is also what is to be enjoyed by this yogin whose self is <s>Bhairava</s>.
And <s>Kumārī</s> is not enjoyed by another; she remains in unity with the enjoyer.
<s>Umā</s>, <s>Kumārī</s>, having abandoned all attachment, is devoted to the worship of the Great Lord.

children.text: ārādhanaparā tadvad icchā śaktis tu yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In just the same way, the yogin's will is his power.
This very clear reading has been seen by the teachers of the unsurpassed.
And it has been explained by others too, on the basis of reading śaktitam eti.
The excellence of this power has been explained as consisting of knowledge and action.
Thus, for the yogin endowed with will-power of such efficacy,

children.text: yad yad dṛśyam aśeṣaṃ tac charīraṃ tasya yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: whatever is visible, without remainder, is the body of that yogin.
For it appears as not separate from 'I', like a husband.
The body, whose form is body, intellect, breath, and emptiness, is like a pot and the like.

children.text: dṛśyam evāsya paśuvat draṣṭṛtvena na bhāsate ||
children.translated_text: For him the visible alone, like a bound creature, appears not as the seer.

children.text: evaṃ dehe ca bāhye ca sarvatraivāsya yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the body and in what is external, everywhere for this yogin,
there is non-different realization, according to the maxim of the peacock's egg and its essence.

children.text: dṛśyaṃ śarīratām eti śarīraṃ cāpi dṛśyatām ||
children.translated_text: The visible becomes the body, and the body too becomes visible.

children.text: ity uktaṃ yogino yat tan na durghaṭam itīryate ||
children.translated_text: What has thus been stated of the yogin is said not to be difficult to accomplish.
Through the impact of mind in the heart, there is the seeing of the sleep of the visible.
One should know that heart to be the great abode of the universe.
According to the principle just stated, the heart, one's own consciousness, is the ground on which the universe rests.

children.text: svasaṃvit tatra saṃghaṭṭaś cittasya calataḥ sataḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, the impact of the mind, while it is moving,
is the wakeful nature born from the reflective awareness of identity with that.
Therefore, of the visible universe, whose form is blue and the body and so on,
there is the perception also of its sleep, that is, of its absence and emptiness.
Among entities in the form of one's own limbs, the knower is called the lord.
Thus, according to the principle stated in the venerable <s>Pratyabhijñā</s>, like a lord or master,
there would be the proper manifestation of it as imagined as his own limbs.
Although this object of knowledge has been stated in this way, another means is now taught.

children.text: śuddhaṃ tattvaṃ paraṃ vastu yat tat paraśivātmakam ||
children.translated_text: The pure principle, the supreme reality, is that whose nature is supreme <s>Śiva</s>.
Union with that is the contemplation of the manifest world as being made of that.

children.text: tenaiva yasya paśvākhyā bandhaśaktir na vidyate ||
children.translated_text: For one in whom, through that very practice, the binding power called animality does not exist,
he, though embodied, is like <s>Sadāśiva</s>, the lord of the entire world.
This belongs only to that yogin who maintains the contemplation of the pure principle.
For the yogin whose bondage has been destroyed by the previously stated union, vitarka is taught:
the reflective consideration, 'I am indeed <s>Śiva</s>, the self of the universe.'

children.text: etad eva sphuradrūpam ātmano jñānam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: This very manifest form is called knowledge of the self.
And further, for him who possesses the aforesaid reflective knowledge of his own self,
the seen, the seer, and the world, in the conscious-yet-unconscious self,
shine forth for the yogin in that world as each taking on its respective form.
Awareness of object and subject is common to all embodied beings.
But this is the distinction of yogins: attentiveness in that relation.

children.text: ity uktanītyā tat sarvam aham ity anusaṃhiteḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because, according to the method just stated, he gathers all that together as 'I,'

children.text: ānando yo bhavaty antas tat samādhisukhaṃ smṛtam ||
children.translated_text: the bliss that arises within is remembered as the happiness of samādhi.
That very happiness of samādhi belonging to the yogin who delights in his own self
is, in the world, the inwardly discovered bliss of people who search within.
Now he shows the yoga of the powers of this yogin.

children.text: icchā śaktir umety ādisūtroktā śaktir asya yā ||
children.translated_text: The śakti (power) of his which is stated in the sūtra beginning 'will is śakti, <s>Umā</s>,'
when the yogin's union with her, his becoming made of her, has occurred,
through her power there is held to be the arising of whatever body is suitable for each particular wish.

children.text: anyāś ca siddhayas tasya sambhavantīty udīryate ||
children.translated_text: And other siddhis (accomplishments) become possible for him, so it is declared.
For beings that are perceiving subjects, empty of body, intellect, and breath,
and for stationary objects that are perceived, union means full nourishment.
Separation, then, is dissociation, for the pacification of afflictions such as disease.
Again, for the universe remote through distance, time, and the like,
contact is such acts as making it directly perceptible to the senses, beginning with the eye.

children.text: etat sarvaṃ bhavec chaktisaṃdhāne sati yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: All this occurs for the yogin when union with śakti has taken place.

children.text: yadā parimitāḥ siddhīr anicchan punar icchati ||
children.translated_text: When, not desiring limited siddhis, he again desires
the supreme siddhi whose form is the manifestation of being the self of the universe, then, for him,
when the yogin seeks the manifestation of universality, he unites his own śakti.
At that time, for him who touches the state of <s>Sadāśiva</s>,
outward opening is <s>Īśvara</s>; inward closing is <s>Sadāśiva</s>.
And the thought 'I am this' is in apposition with true knowledge.

children.text: iti nītyā jagat sarvam aham eveti yā matiḥ ||
children.translated_text: According to this method, the cognition that the whole world is nothing but I

children.text: sā śuddhā nirmalā vidyā tadīyād udayāt sphuṭam ||
children.translated_text: is pure, stainless knowledge; from its arising, clearly,

children.text: unmajjanāt sa cicchaktim ātmano nityam āmṛśet ||
children.translated_text: through its emergence he continually touches his own power of consciousness.

children.text: yadā yogī tadā tasya cakreśatvam anuttaram ||
children.translated_text: At that time, for that yogin, unsurpassed lordship over the circle
and the sovereignty of <s>Maheśvara</s> are accomplished through the excellence of absorption.
When that yogin, whose form is clear consciousness, desires only

children.text: icchati svacchacidrūpo yadā yogī tadāsya tu ||
children.translated_text: to delight in his own self, which is the self of the universe and beyond it, then, for him,
the supreme venerable goddess, consciousness, preceded by the power of will,
emits the inner universe, extending as far as gross objects of knowledge.
Because she sets in motion the streams beginning with <s>Khecarī</s>, whose nature is the senses and their objects,
which are both external and internal and have the form of the inner and outer aspects of the knowing subject,
and because she has qualities such as clarity and profundity,
she is the great lake, pervading the world and beyond the reach of place, time, and the like.
Through inner contemplation of her and through reflective recognition of identity with her,
there is the clear experience of the mantra-power, whose nature is the manifestation of the mass of sounds from a to kṣa,
which agitates within the principles from earth up to <s>Śiva</s>,
which is the life-form of all mantras,
and which consists of the reflective awareness of supreme I-consciousness.

children.text: akhilaṃ vācakaṃ vācyam aham ity avamarśanam ||
children.translated_text: For the attentive yogin, the reflective awareness 'all that expresses and all that is expressed is I'
comes about; this alone remains to be taught.
I shall make clear in brief that object of knowledge which was previously stated.

children.text: mahāhrada iti proktā śaktir bhagavatī parā ||
children.translated_text: The śakti, the blessed supreme one, is called the great lake.
Contemplation is said to be the reflective awareness of identity with that.
Mantra-power is said to be the reflective awareness of full I-consciousness.
Her experience is the clear shining forth of one's own self.
Thus the first opening, devoted to illuminating the <s>Śāmbhava</s> means,
whose mark is the full unfolding of one's own nature, has been properly set forth.
By this one perceives and reflectively apprehends the supreme reality of one's own self.
Thus citta (mind) is the reflective awareness of the shining self, beginning with its radiance.

children.text: tad eva mantryate guptam abhedena vimṛśyate ||
children.translated_text: That very same thing is secretly mantrified, reflectively apprehended as non-different:
'one's own nature is known by this'; therefore the teachers call this a mantra.
Its nature is declared to be the act of contemplation, the flashing forth of full I-consciousness,
and also the property of protection, which brings about the destruction of saṃsāra.
The worshipper's mind, having attained sameness with that through touching the deity of that mantra,
is also a mantra, because it possesses those properties.
And of this mantra just described, whose properties are contemplation and protection,
the effort whose nature is an arising impulse supported by the contemplation of the stated mantra,
an inward self-exertion, is indeed the sādhaka (practitioner).
For it is remembered as granting unity between the one who performs the mantra and the mantra-deity.
The power of the mantra, whose practitioner and goal are of this kind, has first been stated.
Now it is described fully and properly, together with its marks.
It is called <s>vidyā</s>, because its nature is complete realization of supreme nonduality.

children.text: śarīraṃ yasya bhagavān śabdarāśiḥ sa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: That whose body is the blessed mass of sound is so called.
Its being is the form of full I-consciousness that pervades all the courses of manifestation.
That very pulsation is the power of mantras, whose function is reflection and protection.
The production of hidden meaning is called secrecy.
This has been set forth by venerable <s>Kṣemarāja</s>, with correspondences drawn from the <s>Tantrasāra</s>,
and properly described in his own commentary by means of accepted parallels.
Those for whom such mantra-power, just as it really is,
though made known through the method of contemplation on the great lake,
does not become firmly pleasing to the heart solely by the will of <s>Maheśa</s>,

children.text: na gacchaty atha tucchāyāṃ cittaṃ siddhau prarohati ||
children.translated_text: then their mind sprouts toward a trifling attainment.
For those limited yogins, in the accumulation of attainments born from bindu, nāda, and the rest,
the womb is non-recognition, great <s>māyā</s>, made of that very stuff.
The expansion of the mind is then merely the sense of having fulfilled one's purpose in that much alone.
That same undifferentiated <s>vidyā</s> is of the nature of knowing only a little.
That is impure <s>vidyā</s>; it is dream, marked by the cognition of conceptual construction.

children.text: āgatā api tāḥ siddhīḥ khalīkṛtya yadā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But when that yogin again renders even those attained powers ineffectual,

children.text: avaṣṭabhnāty asau yogī parāṃ siddhiṃ tadāśnute ||
children.translated_text: and restrains them, then he obtains the supreme attainment.
By the will of <s>Śaṃkara</s>, when the <s>vidyā</s> whose form was previously described
arises naturally, when it shines forth by its own nature,
and when it emerges, while he is intent on sinking petty attainments,
there is a state of <s>Śiva</s>, not different from the inner state of that one who longs for it.
That very pulsation, whose nature is the overflowing of complete bliss in oneself,

children.text: mudaṃ rātīty ato mudrā khecarī ca nabhaścarī ||
children.translated_text: bestows joy; therefore it is <s>mudrā</s>, and it is <s>khecarī</s>, moving in the ether.
It is manifested everywhere for the yogin whose nature both is the universe and transcends the universe.
Because mantra and mudrā have such power in accomplishing their potency,
the guru declares the true condition of mantra and mudrā, whose life is right knowledge and action,

children.text: gṛṇāty upadiśaty arthaṃ tadvīryaṃ cety ato guruḥ ||
children.translated_text: and teaches their meaning and their power; therefore he is the guru.
That very one, because he reveals the spread of the power of mantras and mudrās,

children.text: upāyaḥ kathyate sākṣād upeyaṃ paramaṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: is directly called the means toward the supreme goal to be attained.

children.text: yad vā guruḥ parā śaktir īśvarānugrahātmikā ||
children.translated_text: Or else the guru is the supreme power, whose nature is the grace of <s>Īśvara</s>.
By granting an opening, that very power comes to be the means.
That guru, equal to myself, is said to be the revealer of mantra-power.
But mantras lacking beginning and end would be like autumn clouds.

children.text: guror lakṣaṇam etāvad ādimāntyaṃ ca vedayet ||
children.translated_text: This much is the mark of the guru: he should make known the beginning and the end.
Thus, because of the greatness taught in the established tantra of the venerable <s>Mālinīśāstra</s>,
from the knower of the beginning and end, whose nature is the unartificial reflective awareness 'I',
from that guru, equal to <s>Parameṣṭhin</s>, the supreme means,
for the practitioner whose mind is constantly intent on contemplation of mantra and mudrā,
this comes about when the aforesaid guru is pleased: so it is taught.
Now the initial lunar days are all the vowels ending in bindu.
At their end, by conjunction with time, the moon and sun are proclaimed.
The tattvas beginning with earth and ending with puruṣa are, in the five
classes beginning with ka and ending with ma, in order, O virtuous one.
The fourfold set of supports belonging to wind, fire, water, and Indra comes next.
Above that is known the group beginning with śa; before it is the fivefold Brahma group.

children.text: amūlā tatkramāj jñeyā kṣāntā sṛṣṭir udāhṛtā ||
children.translated_text: Having no root, this creation is to be understood in that sequence and is said to end with kṣa.

children.text: sarveṣāṃ caiva mantrāṇāṃ vidyānāṃ ca yaśasvini ||
children.translated_text: For all mantras and for all <s>vidyās</s>, O illustrious one,
this is always declared in all tantras to be the womb.
Thus, according to the principle taught in the venerable <s>Triśikāśāstra</s>, the <s>mātṛkā</s>
contains within it the sixteen vowels from a to visarga.
Therefore its order of fifteen lunar days extends from the beginning to bindu.
It is adorned with the pair of bindus that both consists of that and transcends that.

children.text: ata eva jagat sarvaṃ sṛjaty antar anuttare ||
children.translated_text: Therefore within the unsurpassed it creates the entire universe.
Within that set of fifteen, by means of the five vowels drawn out,

children.text: a i u ṛ ﾱ vinyāsaiḥ kādimāntaṃ ca vācakam ||
children.translated_text: a, i, u, ṛ, and ḷ, through their arrangements, express the series from ka through ma,
and the cluster of tattvas to be expressed, beginning with earth and ending with puruṣa.
By division into five pentads, it unfolds as five times five.

children.text: bahiś cānuttarād eva sṛjatī viśvam īdṛśam ||
children.translated_text: And externally too, from the unsurpassed alone, it creates such a universe.
The sounds ya, ra, la, and va respectively embody wind, fire, water, and Indra.
They arise from the mutual conjunction of the triad called unsurpassed, will, and opening.
Moreover, by the force of the conjunction of the pair called unsurpassed and neuter,
there arise those named kalā, vidyā, māyā, and rāga.
By concealing their own form and removing omnipotence and the rest,
they grant a little agency and the like to the fragmented bound soul.
Because the ascent above māyā to the tattvas beginning with pure vidyā is blocked,
and because the descent below the root is also blocked, like <s>Triśaṅku</s>,
this one is established in the middle by the supports whose nature is support.
Restriction is what gives rise to the arrangement of existent and nonexistent things.
Even time follows that great <s>māyā</s>, which is independent.
So, according to this statement, because they are joined with time and restriction, they have a sixfold nature.
After expanding the body, above that is the fivefold group beginning with śa,
the Brahma-form extending from <s>Sadyojāta</s> through <s>Īśāna</s>,
made of the subtle forms of earth, water, fire, wind, and ether.
in due order, whose nature is pure knowledge, the Lord, <s>Sadāśiva</s>, <s>Śakti</s>, and <s>Śiva</s>.
By the digit of emission she unfolds outward what is stationed within herself.
Since even the final letter kṣa is contained within the letters from ka to sa,
therefore, by the letters a and ha, as the inseparable word "I",
it shines forth, enclosing the manifest world with <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Śakti</s>.

children.text: asyās tv evaṃprabhāvāyāś cakraṃ yat tad ihoditam ||
children.translated_text: The circle of her, who has such power, is taught here:
a cluster of powers of vibration beginning with the unsurpassed, will, and opening forth.
Awakening to that is recollection of one's own self, compact with consciousness and bliss.
Now, for one whose self has been awakened by awakening to such a circle of the mothers,

children.text: śūnyaṃ dhīḥ prāṇa ity etat sṛjyate kṣīyate 'pi ca ||
children.translated_text: emptiness, intellect, and breath are created, and they also perish.

children.text: sthairyam asti paraṃ dehāpekṣayā na tu tattvataḥ ||
children.translated_text: They have supreme stability in relation to the body, but not in ultimate reality.

children.text: ity uktanītyā śūnyādeḥ pramātā tv asya bhittibhūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, according to the principle stated, the knower of emptiness and the rest is the ground of this.
The gross, subtle, and other body of the supreme yogin,
when offered into the fire of consciousness, is called the oblation, because it sinks into identity with that knower.
It gives rise to the knower whose self is full manifestation of light.
Thus, by the oblation that is the body, for him whose upward flame is blazing awareness,

children.text: jñānaṃ bandha iti proktaṃ yat prāk tat parayoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: what was previously called "knowledge is bondage" applies to the supreme yogin.

children.text: anātmany ātmatājñaptir annaṃ grasyata ity ataḥ ||
children.translated_text: The cognition of selfhood in what is not self is food that is swallowed; therefore,
moreover, whatever has the nature of reflective awareness of the essence that is light,
that knowledge is called food, because it produces supreme delight.

children.text: yadā tv avahitaḥ śaśvad yogī naivaṃ bhavaty asau ||
children.translated_text: But when the yogin is constantly attentive, he does not become like this.
Then, even though he possesses knowledge, because of the pride of concentration,
the knowledge called <s>vidyā</s>, whose form is the expansion of knowledge and which was stated before,
as pure knowledge, when it is not arisen in dissolution and sinks down,
then from the successive birth of the manifest knowledge that has arisen from it and is being dissolved,
there is the perception of dream, fixed in difference, a flood of conceptual constructions.
This becomes the arising of him whose highest self was explained earlier,
when the practitioner is proud in his attention; so it is taught.
Thus ends the second opening, which illuminates the <s>śāktopāya</s> (method of power).
Having the form of an entrance of latent impressions of particular enjoyables, sound and the rest,
inclined toward the operation of instruments such as each particular determination,
supported by the functions of sattva and the other guṇas, and consisting of intellect, ego-maker, and mind,
that is called <s>citta</s>, because it fails to reflect upon the taught nature of consciousness.
According to each of its actions it goes on into various wombs;

children.text: atatīty ata evātmā tataḥ so 'ṇuḥ prakīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: because it does not pass beyond, for that very reason the self is therefore called atomic.
There is no absence of consciousness in the self, whose sole nature is awareness.
Therefore consciousness is the self; this, consisting of cognition and activity,
is declared to be the real form of the self, which is the nature of the universe.
Now, because of contraction manifested by this self's own freedom,
and because of connection with atomicity, <s>citta</s> is defined as the self.
Thus there is no inconsistency at all between the earlier and later teachings.

children.text: asya cittasvarūpasya dehāder ātmanas tv aṇoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Of this nature of <s>citta</s>, and of the body and so on belonging to the self as atomic,
within there are functions such as determination, with happiness and the like as objects of experience,
while outside it is turned toward suitable objects such as blue, the body, and the like.
Its knowledge, whose nature is the appearance of difference, is bondage for the atomic form.
Precisely because he is bound by that, this atomic self certainly transmigrates.

children.text: jñānaṃ prakāśakaṃ loke ātmā caiva prakāśakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Knowledge is illuminative in the world, and the self too is illuminative.
Because these two are inseparable, the knower shines forth in knowledge.
According to the principle just stated, knowledge illuminates its own nature;
like the self, how then can the condition of its being a binder arise?

children.text: ity āśaṅkyāha yady evaṃ prasannāt parameśvarāt ||
children.translated_text: Anticipating this objection, he says: if this recognition arises from the gracious Supreme Lord,

children.text: pratyabhijñā bhavaty eṣā tadā satyaṃ tvadīritam ||
children.translated_text: then what you have said is true.
But when this reflective awareness is not present for him because of that Lord's power of māyā,
then, from the innermostly flashing entities that grant limited agency and the like,
from the tattvas beginning with <s>kalā</s> and ending with earth, whose nature is the sheaths,
standing as the eightfold subtle city and as the gross body and the rest,
non-discrimination among them is the continued apprehension of them as self.
That itself is deluding māyā, the world consisting in the non-recognition of reality.
Therefore, for the pacification of this māyā born from it, for this yogin,
in the gross body made of the great elements, in the subtle body whose self is the eightfold city,
and in the body extending from the root up to <s>samanā</s>, for the supreme yogin,

children.text: kalānāṃ tatra bhāgānāṃ kāryāṇāṃ kāraṇe nije ||
children.translated_text: the dissolution there of the <s>kalās</s>, the portions, the effects, into their own cause,
is the existence of the single fire of awareness, through contemplation of dissolution.
Or it is to be meditated upon by the method of reflective awareness such as burning; so it is taught.
Thus the means of dissolution called meditation has been stated.
In this way, he shows these principal means, preceded by breath-control,
and other means extending up to concentration.
They are to be cultivated by a disciplined practitioner; so it is taught.
The dissolution of the channels that carry breath and the rest is by restraint of breath.
Through the production of the sequence beginning with exhalation, in the fire whose self is <s>udāna</s>,
one brings about their being dissolved in the central channel, because they become identical with that.

children.text: bhūtānāṃ bhūjalādīnāṃ jayo yaḥ sa udīryate ||
children.translated_text: The mastery of the elements, earth, water, and the rest, is what is declared.
The airy fixation is in the thumb; the fiery one is from the middle of the navel.
The earthy one is in the region of the throat, while the watery one rests in the uvula.
The fixation on space is at the crown of the head and is remembered as producing all accomplishments.
Thus mastery is obtained through the dhāraṇās taught in the <s>Svacchandaśāstra</s>.
From the elements, indeed, comes isolation; from that, the withdrawal of mind.
Separation is distinctness, the pure single form of one's own self, unstained by that.
The result formerly taught in sūtras such as 'joining with the elements'
is accomplished without effort by one endowed with the <s>Śāmbhava</s> means.
But what is to be accomplished by the <s>Āṇava</s> means is distinguished as requiring effort.

children.text: ity evaṃ dehaśuddhyādyaiḥ samādhyantaiś ca yā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: Thus the siddhi that may arise through bodily purification and the other practices up to samādhi
is said to come from the covering of delusion, not from knowledge of the self.
Delusion is <s>māyā</s>, the bewildering power; because of the covering produced by it, indeed,
siddhi through the previously mentioned methods such as dhāraṇā is limited.
It consists in the enjoyment of each particular tattva, not in the manifestation of supreme consciousness for this person.
But for one whose entrance into delusion has been destroyed, again, ahead in samādhi,
having resorted to the middle prāṇa, the interval between the paths of prāṇa and apāna,

children.text: ālambya jñānaśaktiṃ ca tatsthaṃ caivāsanaṃ labhet ||
children.translated_text: and having taken support from the power of knowledge, he would obtain the seat established there.
Abandoning the gross condition beginning with prāṇa, then the subtle inner condition,

children.text: sūkṣmātītaṃ tu paramaṃ spandanaṃ labhyate yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: one attains the supreme vibration beyond the subtle.

children.text: prāṇāyāmaḥ sa uddiṣṭo yasmān na cyavate punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That is designated prāṇāyāma, since from it one does not fall away again.
The activity of qualities such as sound is indeed experienced by the mind.

children.text: tyaktvā tāṃ paramaṃ dhāma praviśet tatsvacetasā ||
children.translated_text: Abandoning that, one should enter the supreme abode with one's own mind.
This is called pratyāhāra, the cutter of the bonds of becoming.
Having transcended the qualities of intellect, one should meditate on the object of meditation, undiminishing and all-pervading.

children.text: dhyātvā dhyeyaṃ svasaṃvedyaṃ dhyānaṃ tac ca vidur budhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The wise know that meditation as an object of meditation directly known by oneself.
That by which supreme selfhood is always held
is specified as dhāraṇā, the destroyer of the bondage of becoming.
Toward beings located in oneself and in others, in this world, one whose understanding is equal thinks,

children.text: śivo 'ham advitīyo 'haṃ samādhiḥ sa paraḥ smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'I am <s>Śiva</s>; I am non-dual.' That is remembered as the supreme samādhi.
Thus, by the stages explained by the venerable <s>Mṛtyujittantra</s>,
beginning with restraint of prāṇa and extending up to samādhi,
entrance into the supreme reality certainly takes place, so it is said.
Delusion is <s>māyā</s>, the non-recognition of oneself; through its conquest, through its defeat,
the infinite one arises like the rising sun, up to the calming of latent impressions.
For the yogin whose expansion and extent are such, whose self has been shown in this way,
there arises the conquest, the attainment, of innate knowledge.
Thus, when the great rising of pure knowledge has been obtained through the conquest of delusion,
having thus partaken of innate knowledge and relying on unity with that alone,

children.text: jāgarūkaḥ sadā yogī jāgrad ity ayam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: the yogin who is always awake is called this 'waking' one.
In relation to his own I-ness, whose nature is the reflective awareness of complete I-consciousness, the world,

children.text: dvitīyam idam ākāraṃ karo yasya svadīdhitiḥ ||
children.translated_text: this second form, is a ray of his own radiance.
Being such, he becomes one for whom the world has been made his own possession.
Such a one, whose mind is always entered into the reflective awareness of his own self,
dances within, supported by the forms of his own nature that are delimited.
By his own will, on the wall of his own consciousness, through the play of his own vibration,
he illumines those various levels of his, whose forms are waking, dream, and deep sleep.

children.text: ābhāsayati yat tasmād ātmā nartaka ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Because he manifests them, the self is called the dancer.
For this yogin, the dancer in the world-drama of such a kind,
the teacher of the world states the place for assuming the levels to be the stage.
Because the self, delighting in the sport of the world-drama, is colored in it,
therefore the inner self, the living being constituted by the eightfold subtle body, is the stage.
The yogin, having taken his place there, through the play of the vibration of his own senses,
manifests the world-drama extending from <s>Sadāśiva</s> down to earth.
As he dances on this stage, the inner space of the body, in his own inner self,
the body that makes manifest the drama of saṃsāra is called the spectators.
The senses beginning with the eye wonder inwardly for the yogin.
Thus, for the yogin whose own circle of senses has become the spectator,
intellect, the mind skillful in the reflective awareness whose form is true consciousness,
by that very power, for the sattva, the vibration turning within,
siddhi, the manifestation whose form is flashing forth, clearly arises.
Thus, from the splendor of attaining the sattva whose nature is his own flashing forth,
this supreme yogin becomes siddha, indeed perfected.
His independent state is marked by innate knowing and agency.
The autonomy of the master is capable of bringing the universe under his own control.
For him, whose self is filled with his own bliss, this independent state alone
is freedom made manifest in the natural body.

children.text: yathā tatra tathānyatra dehe bhavati yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: As it is there, so it comes to be in another body for the yogin.
For the one who is joined, the form of complete I-consciousness becomes manifest.

children.text: na caivam apy udāsīnena bhāvyaṃ yogināpi tu ||
children.translated_text: Yet even so, the yogin must not remain indifferent.

children.text: sphurattātmā parā śaktir bījaṃ viśvasya kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: The supreme śakti, whose nature is flashing forth, is the seed, the cause of the universe.
Attention to that, the repeated placing of the mind there,
must be done carefully by the yogin; this is what is taught.
Such a great yogin, attentive to the supreme śakti,
abides, stands, in that with unity; therefore it is called āsana.

children.text: śāktaṃ balaṃ yat tatrasthas tadevāntaḥ parāmṛśan ||
children.translated_text: The śākta power that is there, while established in it and inwardly reflectively apprehending just that,
the yogin has cast off the exertion of meditation, dhāraṇā, and the like.
It is the cause of the flowing expansion of the great current beginning with <s>Khecarī</s>.
In the lake endowed with qualities such as clarity and filled with his own bliss,
in the island of the word 'this,' flooded and complete within the ocean of consciousness,
having cast aside every means, he immerses himself there at will.
Precisely by the sinking down of the body and the rest, he clearly becomes identical with that.
Thus, from the conquest of delusion attained through the <s>āṇava-upāya</s> (individual means),
through the excellence of <s>śākta</s> absorption, whose nature is the rising of pure knowledge,
and from a deep plunging into the lake of supreme bliss made one's own,
the highest practitioner possesses the splendor that is subject to the manifesting <s>Śāmbhava</s> state.
The measure belonging to himself, of consciousness whose form has been described,
is a congealed, limited portion of the self, marked by object and subject.
The bringing forth of its construction, and the seeing of it as constructed,
the lordly yogin accomplishes clearly, at will, by his own intention.
Thus, for the yogin whose universal form arises from such a śakti,
there is said to be no connection at all with rebirth and the like.
For him this innate knowledge is the perpetual rise that is not destroyed.
By that very fact, for this aggregate of body, breath, intellect, and the rest,
which is joined to the several actions accompanied by ignorance,
the destruction of birth, the eradication of the root, takes place for him. This remains to be taught.

children.text: yadā tu śuddhavidyāyāḥ svarūpaṃ tasya majjati ||
children.translated_text: But when the essential nature of pure knowledge sinks down for him,
then the śaktis rise up precisely to delude him.
They stand in the groups beginning with ka and have become their presiding powers,
the powers beginning with <s>Māheśvarī</s>, situated in the midst of the consciousness of the apertures mentioned before.
Entering the bound subjects, the cognizers, in the respective grounds of their cognitions,
and deluding them by penetration through the corresponding words, they are the mothers of bound beings.
Concealing their own form, whose nature is a solid mass of consciousness and bliss,
and revealing excessive self-regard toward the body and the like, even though inert,
these powers delude even the practitioner who, like a bound being, has become heedless.
Therefore this yogin must always be in a state of cultivation, with careful attention.
For it has been said in general that the support of knowledge is the <s>mātṛkā</s>.

children.text: idaṃ tu prāptatattvo 'pi pramādyan sādhakaḥ punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But this means that even a practitioner who has attained reality, if he becomes heedless again,
is deluded by the mothers who are the supports of bound beings.

children.text: yata evam ataḥ śuddhavidyā prāptāpi yuktibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since this is so, therefore, although pure knowledge has been attained by many methods,

children.text: bahvībhiḥ sā punar mauḍhyādy athāsya na vinaśyati ||
children.translated_text: for him it does not again perish because of dullness and the like,

children.text: tathā sarvāsv avasthāsu yukto bhūyād itīryate ||
children.translated_text: provided that he remains joined with it in all states; so it is declared.
'In the three' means in those whose forms have been stated, waking and the rest, like oil.
The fourth, previously mentioned, whose nature is the expansion of pure knowledge,

children.text: turyaṃ dhāma sadāsecyaṃ yathā syāt tanmayaṃ trayam ||
children.translated_text: is the abode called <s>turya</s>; it is always to be served, so that the three become identical with it.

children.text: yathā tailaṃ kramāt svīyam āśrayaṃ vyāpnuyāt tathā ||
children.translated_text: Just as oil gradually pervades its own support, so too
at the beginning and ending points, clearly shining forth in waking and the rest,
one should moisten even the middle state with the sap of the bliss of <s>turya</s>.
By the sūtra beginning 'waking,' it was previously taught that, through exertion,
for the supreme yogin endowed with attentive union with the circle of śaktis,
within the grounds of waking, dream, and deep sleep spreading by their own taste,
there arises the expansion of <s>turya</s>, issuing forth of itself.
By the sūtra beginning 'the triad,' from the forceful ripening process accomplished by the <s>Śāmbhava</s> means,
the withdrawal of waking, dream, and deep sleep was shown.
But by this sūtra, according to the method of the <s>āṇava-upāya</s>,
the three states beginning with waking, abiding as if they were petals,
are to be sprinkled with the sap of <s>turya</s>; this distinction is set forth.
Here he again states the means for sprinkling them with the nectar of <s>turya</s>.
Having abandoned gross and conceptual means such as breath-control,
with one's own mind and one's own consciousness, whose form is nonconceptual,
whose nature is the relish of the wonder of inward reflective awareness,
one should be immersed here in the sap of <s>turya</s>, and by that immersion
calming one's subjecthood connected with one's own body and the rest, one should enter it, become absorbed in it.
In this way, when the yogin's intellect has entered the supreme state,

children.text: yadā bhūyaḥ prasaraṇaṃ yogino jāyate tadā ||
children.translated_text: and when, by the nature of reality, expansion again occurs for him, then
as the breath expands, refined by absorption into the fragrance of the manifesting śakti,
through the power of an intellect supported by all the knots, fully opened,

children.text: īṣad bahir mandamandaṃ cāre prasaraṇe sati ||
children.translated_text: when it moves outward slightly and expands very gently,
because it has the nature of a solid mass of consciousness, there is equally, at all times, a vision of non-difference.
The yogin's awareness naturally exists in all states.
If, while attaining support in <s>turya</s>, he does not reflectively touch <s>turyātīta</s> (that beyond turya),
and remains in mere <s>turya</s>, experienced at the prior and posterior endpoints,

children.text: āste yogī tadāmuṣya tāvan mātreṇa tuṣyataḥ ||
children.translated_text: then that yogin, satisfied with just that much of it, stays there.
For the yogin who serves <s>turya</s> at the earlier and later endpoints,
but is proud in his attention, there may at some time
fall upon the middle point a lower, not superior, contemptible creation.

children.text: vyutthānātmā tato yogī sāvadhānaḥ sadā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: It has the nature of emergence into ordinary activity; therefore the yogin should always be attentive.

children.text: avaraprasave vṛtte hy evaṃ madhyapade punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For when an inferior production has thus occurred again in the middle state,
from the relish of support in <s>turya</s> he should reflectively touch <s>turyātīta</s>.

children.text: mātrāḥ padārthāḥ rūpādyās tāsv ebhiś cakṣurādibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The measures are objects, such as forms and the rest; among them, by these faculties beginning with the eye,
the so-called cognition of each is the knowing of its own respective object.

children.text: saṃdhānaṃ tu samastaṃ tad aham ity anusaṃhitiḥ ||
children.translated_text: But the linking together of all that is the continuing awareness 'I.'
When this has perished in him, because it has been carried off by the aforesaid group,

children.text: turyasya punar utthānaṃ bhūya unmajjanaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: The rising again of the fourth state is a further emerging upward.
It is taught as the fullness of the sovereign yogin's attainment of unity with that.
Thus the bull among practitioners, in whom the excellence of rising immersion is increasing,
through the excellence of practice of the fourth state, reaches the state whose nature is beyond the fourth.
The practitioner who has directly attained it becomes, as the inner self of all worlds,
equal to <s>Śiva</s>, who consists of consciousness, is pure, self-willed, and endowed with bliss.
Because the portion of the body has not fallen away, he is equal; when it does fall away, he is <s>Śiva</s>.
What was acquired has been burned by initiation; future karmas, beginning with restraint,
by which this has been accomplished, cease through the experience of that wherein it occurs.
Karma belonging to many lives is burned like a seed by fire.

children.text: bhaviṣyad api saṃruddhaṃ yenedaṃ taddhi bhogataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Even future karma is obstructed; and what remains, by which this body persists, is removed through experience.
By the rule thus stated, the continued existence of his body,
as the ground for experiencing the enjoyments that have come through begun karma, is taught as something to be performed.
Thus, by the method stated before, for the yogin who is equal to <s>Śiva</s>,
whose supreme self is intent on worship of his own self, eternally of the nature of <s>Śiva</s>,
nourished within by the nectar of clear and pure devotion that shines forth,
'May this body of mine exist for use in your worship' -
in accordance with this direction spoken by the transcendent and glorious <s>Utpala</s>,
whatever continuance he has in a body filled with the nectar of devotion to <s>Śiva</s>,

children.text: vratam etad anuṣṭheyaṃ na tucchaṃ tasya dhāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: that is the vow to be undertaken; its preservation is not trivial.
For such a one, whatever takes the form of his own free utterance,
'I praise your form, made of great mantra, pure and cool,
lovely with unprecedented fragrance and rich with the flavor of the supreme nectar' -
according to this direction spoken by the teacher, the maker of the venerable <s>Pratyabhijñā</s>,
for one who reflects on his own self, made of the uncontrived awareness 'I am,'
whatever discourse consists of free utterance and speaks reality as it is,

children.text: bhūyobhūyaḥ pare bhāve bhāvanā bhāvyate hi yā ||
children.translated_text: whatever contemplation is repeatedly cultivated in the supreme state,

children.text: japaḥ so 'tra svayaṃ nādo mantrātmā japya īdṛśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: that itself here is <s>japa</s> (recitation), spontaneous sound, mantra in essence, and such is what is to be recited.
Six hundred and twenty-one thousand repetitions in a day and night

children.text: japo devyāḥ samuddiṣṭaḥ sulabho durlabho jaḍaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: are prescribed for the goddess; this is easy, though hard for dull people.
By the rule thus stated, because that wealth of reflective awareness whose lord is the self of all
has the property of generating and preserving, it is called <s>japa</s>.
And whatever discourse has as its subject a yogin of such a kind,
that too is called <s>japa</s> for people, because it is connected with generation and preservation.
Now his <s>caryā</s> (conduct), which conforms to proper bounds, is also described.
The direct realization of the self whose form is the consciousness just stated -

children.text: yat taj jñānaṃ tad evāsya dānaṃ yatnena dīyate ||
children.translated_text: that is knowledge, and that very thing is his gift, given with effort.

children.text: paripūrṇaṃ svarūpaṃ svaṃ dīyate khaṇḍyate bhidā ||
children.translated_text: His own complete nature is given; division is cut off.

children.text: dāyate śodhyate rūpam ātmīyaṃ dīyate punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: His own form is bestowed and purified; again it is given.
The self, recognized as the <s>Śiva</s>-self by its own nature, is protected.
And so, with effort, the unsurpassed knowledge of the self is given.
Through compassion he gives that to his own pupils as his very self.

children.text: evaṃ samyagvrataṃ proktaṃ japaṃ caryā ca pālayan ||
children.translated_text: Thus, while observing the rightly taught vow, recitation, and conduct,
being equal to <s>Śiva</s> and always intent on the worship of his own self as <s>Śiva</s>,
this very great yogin is the bearer of the burden of the great mantra,
the one who teaches reality in truth within the community of resident pupils.
Thus speaks the blessed Lord, <s>Īśa</s>, who constantly bestows grace.
Because it protects the unknowing herd of bound beings, the circle of powers is called <s>avipa</s>.
Beginning with <s>Māheśvarī</s>, it is taught as the presiding divinity over the consonant groups beginning with ka.

children.text: adhitiṣṭhati yaḥ svairam avipasthaḥ sa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: He who freely presides over it is called one established in <s>avipa</s>.

children.text: jānātīty akhilaṃ tat jñā jñānaśaktir udīryate ||
children.translated_text: Because it knows all, it is called 'the knower'; it is declared to be the power of knowledge.

children.text: tasyā hetus tayā śiṣyān pratibodhayituṃ kṣamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Being the cause of that, by means of it he is able to awaken his pupils.
But another person, because he has been made dependent by the wheel of powers,

children.text: svātmany evāsamarthaḥ san katham anyān prabodhayet ||
children.translated_text: being powerless even in his own self, how could he awaken others?
With reference to the word 'which' in the sūtra, the word 'that' is supplied of itself.

children.text: caśabdo hy arthavācy atra yasmāj jñānaprabodhane ||
children.translated_text: The word 'and' here expresses the reason: because in the awakening of knowledge

children.text: yogī hetus tato dānam ātmajñānam itīritam ||
children.translated_text: the yogin is the cause, therefore the gift is said to be knowledge of the self.

children.text: ity evam avipasthasya jñāhetor asya yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, for this yogin established in <s>avipa</s>, who is the cause of knowledge,

children.text: śaktayo 'sya jagat kṛtsnaṃ śaktimāṃs tu maheśvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: the powers are his entire universe, while the possessor of powers is the great Lord.
As, according to the direction of the āgama, the universe is the accumulation of <s>Śiva</s>'s own powers,
so too, for this supreme yogin who is equal to him, it is likewise.
Of his own power, never separated from his own self and consisting of awareness,
the accumulation, whose form is flashing forth, is held to be the expansion that is the universe.
Not only in the state of creation, for this supreme yogin,
is the universe the accumulation of his own power; as far as that extends, the two that follow it,
the accumulations of his own power, are also stated, and this carries forward.
Of the universe expanded by his own consciousness consisting of action,
there is, with regard to the respective perceivers, for some time, a state of objectivity.

children.text: yā sthitiś cinmayāhaṃtāviśrāntyātmā ca yo layaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That is its maintenance; and the dissolution is rest in the consciousness-made 'I'-ness.
Both of these, for that yogin, consist in the accumulation of his own power.

children.text: vikasat saṃkucat sarvaṃ vedyaṃ yat saṃvidātmakam ||
children.translated_text: Everything knowable, expanding and contracting, has the nature of consciousness,
because otherwise the cognition of that knowable thing would be impossible.
But, one may object, in creation, maintenance, and destruction, which are thus mutually distinct,
a difference in the yogin's own nature would result.
To remove this doubt, the great Lord states the sūtra.
Even while those states such as creation are continually in operation,
and even while they emerge, he possesses the support of unwavering yoga.
Here this pair of states is called being an effect and being an agent.

children.text: kāryatā kṣayiṇī tatra kartṛtvaṃ punar akṣayam ||
children.translated_text: Among these, being an effect is perishable, but agency is imperishable.

children.text: kāryonmukhaḥ prayatno yaḥ kevalaṃ so 'tra lupyate ||
children.translated_text: Only that effort which is turned toward an effect is lost here.
When that has been lost, the unawakened person understands, "I have been lost."
But the inward-turned state, which is the basis of the quality of omniscience,
can never be lost, because no other thing is apprehended.
Thus, according to the method stated in the venerable <s>Spandaśāstra</s>, for this yogin
there is no rejection, since he does not fall away from his own nature as self-knower,
because of the wonder of the rising <s>turya</s> and because he has the nature of the apprehender.
If that creation and the rest were rejected, even what is to be created would not shine forth.
For the yogin who is unshaken in the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe,
for the wise one who has transcended the knowerhood belonging to body, breath, and the rest,
his conquering of contact with what is to be known is the contemplation of pleasure and pain
externally, in the form of the appearance of this-ness, like blue, yellow, and the rest.

children.text: ahaṃ sukhīti duḥkhīti lokavan na tv ahaṃtayā ||
children.translated_text: He thinks, like ordinary people, "I am happy" or "I am unhappy," but not through real I-ness.
According to the principle of the sūtra, "The universe is the unfolding of one's own powers,"
everything appears to him as covered by I-ness.

children.text: yogino laukikasyeva sukhādy eva na kevalam ||
children.translated_text: For the yogin, as for an ordinary person, it is not merely pleasure and the like.
Since he has passed beyond the ego-making of body and the rest, which is overwhelmed by great delusion,
how could the king of yogins be touched by pleasure and pain as ordinary people are?
Because the knowerhood of consciousness rises forth, while the condition of the eightfold subtle body sinks down,

children.text: yato na tatsukhādyantas tata evaiṣa sādhakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: therefore he is not included within pleasure and the rest; for that very reason this practitioner

children.text: tābhyāṃ mukto viśeṣeṇa yogīndro yat tayor yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: is especially free from those two, O lord of yogins, since from them
he is untouched even by latent impression, and is remembered as isolated, consisting of consciousness alone.
The word "but" declares a distinction with reference to what is going to be said.
So too, the word in the following sūtra has reference to this sūtra.
That very distinction expressed by the word "but" is stated by <s>Candraśekhara</s>.

children.text: mohaḥ svākhyātir ajñānaṃ tena yaḥ pratisaṃhataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Delusion is the non-declaration of one's own nature, ignorance; one who is contracted by it,
having reached compact identity with that alone, thereafter becomes the support of pain and the rest.
For that very reason he is of the nature of karma, stained by good and bad.
Even for this very one, such as he is, whose nature is those respective karmas, when
the innate union with freedom, opening forth through the unobstructed descent of <s>Maheśāna</s>'s power,
becomes manifest, then for him, however,
when the difference born from the limited egoity of body, breath, and the rest,
whose nature is suited to the limited subject and others, deluded as it is enclosed by <s>kalā</s> and the rest,
is obscured, and even though it remains, is thrust aside by his own opening forth,
because the identity with mantra and lord of mantra and the greatness of his own self are revealed,
there may arise in this supreme yogin the agency of another creation.
His evident capacity to create what is to be measured according to his desire would become manifest.

children.text: na caitad apy asaṃbhāvyaṃ sraṣṭṛtvaṃ yogino yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor is even this creatorship of the yogin impossible, because
from his own experience, from himself, in dreams, acts of imagination, and the like,
the instrument is the production of objects known by his own awareness and of the grasper and the grasped.
The power, the opening forth of agency in that, is established by self-awareness itself.

children.text: sambhavantīṃ tathā sṛṣṭiṃ yadi dārḍhyena bhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: If he would contemplate such possible creation with firmness,
then there would also be the entire creation common to all.
For here, through the power that is the instrument, power has the form of freedom.
It is the essence of the knowing subject whose nature is awareness; therefore, by his own māyā,
in order to stimulate the power of freedom that has been concealed,
the threefold state of waking, dream, and deep sleep, in sequence,
has been explained indirectly as having, in each case, the form of beginning, middle, and end.
It consists of orientation toward an object, attachment to it, and unification with that alone,
and has the form of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, with <s>turya</s> itself as its beginning.
The end of those three has as its nature a mass of the bliss of the flavor of wonder.
Though covered by māyā, whose nature is concealment,
in the enjoyment of each particular object it flashes for a moment like lightning.
The practitioner should, by attention, produce its enlivening.
By that very life, he should also properly stimulate
the life of his own self, through which he may become identical with it.
The enlivening by <s>turya</s> was earlier taught with regard to the three states beginning with waking
by the sūtra, "the fourth," and by this phrase beginning "threefold state."
It is specified as occurring in the joints that are the beginning, middle, and end of waking and the rest.
It is not only in the state whose nature is inward-turned

children.text: tripadādiprāṇanam ity etad uktam athāpi tu ||
children.translated_text: that this enlivening of the threefold state and so on has been stated; rather,

children.text: anuprāṇanam ity etad ādadyād iti śiṣyate ||
children.translated_text: the phrase "should produce enlivening" is to be supplied.
Just as in the state of mind whose nature is inward-turned, so too
by the liberated <s>turya</s>, whose nature is bliss and which consists in enlivening,
he should make everything identical with that even in outwardness, whose nature is body, senses, and objects.

children.text: tanmayaṃ bhavatīty arthāt tadā sarvaṃ carācaram ||
children.translated_text: Since that is the meaning, then all that moves and does not move
is in this way his power, whose nature is his own bliss and whose mark is freedom.
It plainly becomes capable of creating objects at will.

children.text: yadā punar asau yogī proktāṃ turyātmikāṃ daśām ||
children.translated_text: But when that yogin does not inwardly touch
the stated inner condition whose nature is <s>turya</s>, then, because of the egoity of body and the rest,
which has the form of considering what is incomplete to be other, and whose nature is the atomic impurity,
By the tattvas beginning with <s>kalā</s> and ending with earth, which are overrun by hosts of powers,

children.text: yoner yonyantaraṃ neyaḥ saṃvāhyaḥ paśur ucyate ||
children.translated_text: the bound soul is said to be carried and led from one womb to another womb.
For him, whose form is the atomic impurity and who follows each particular action,
there is outward movement because of desire, whose form is incompleteness and otherness.
His condition is only being turned toward objects; there is no inner joining with the tattvas.
But when, under the power of the descent of <s>Maheśāna</s>'s power,

children.text: ātmīyam eva vimṛśan nāste rūpaṃ tadāsya tu ||
children.translated_text: he reflects only upon what is his own, then for him that form does not remain.
Because desire is absent, no outward movement would occur.
Rather, it is said to be precisely the previously described delighting in one's own self.
In that abode, referred to by the word 'that' and whose nature is being the conscious subject,
the cognition that has ascended there is consciousness, intent upon reflective awareness of that.
For the one whose cognition is like this, there is the destruction of the soul, so it has been said,
through the decay of the established verbalization belonging to the atomic impurity,
and in reality the pacification of what has the nature of the eightfold city occurs.
But if the soul is destroyed in this way, then the falling away of his body would result.
Yet this is never seen in the case of anyone, even of a yogin here.
Therefore how could he be a practitioner whose cognition has ascended to that?
Having anticipated this objection, the blessed teacher of the universe gives the answer.
When there is the destruction of the soul through the pacification of the desire just mentioned,
even though the conceit of being the knower in the eightfold city melts away, he,
untouched in the 'I'-state by the elements that have begun the body,
is, like one wearing a sheath, especially liberated because he has the fortune of nirvāṇa.
Again, in abundant measure, this one is equal to the Lord, the supreme ruler,
having the dense nature of consciousness and bliss, immersed in that one's own nature.

children.text: tata eva paraḥ pūrṇaḥ samyak tanmayatāṃ gataḥ ||
children.translated_text: For that very reason he is supreme, full, and has fully entered into identity with that.
Even so, his being sheathed by the elements does not cease at that very time.

children.text: kasmād ity api śaṅkāyām uttaraṃ vakti śaṃkaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: When there is also the question 'why?', <s>Śaṃkara</s> gives the answer.

children.text: prāṇe pariṇatā saṃvit prāg iti proktayā diśā ||
children.translated_text: Consciousness has transformed into breath, according to the previously stated method.
By its own innate, natural, unobstructed freedom,
with the wish to produce the excellence of the variegated moving world,
the blessed consciousness itself, taking on contraction,
reaches the levels that grasp each particular contracted breath.

children.text: uktam arthaṃ dṛḍhīkartuṃ saṃvādaḥ so 'yam atra tu ||
children.translated_text: Here this agreement is given in order to make firm the meaning that has been stated.

children.text: yā sā śaktiḥ parā sūkṣmā vyāpinī nirmalā śivā ||
children.translated_text: That power which is supreme, subtle, all-pervading, stainless, and auspicious,
the mother of the wheel of powers, whose self is the nectar of supreme bliss,
the great terrible Lady, fierce, maker of creation and dissolution,

children.text: trivahaṃ trividhaṃ triṣṭhaṃ balāt kālaṃ prakarṣati ||
children.translated_text: forcibly draws time, which has three streams, three forms, and stands in three ways.

children.text: iti vājasaneyāyām iyam eva citiḥ parā ||
children.translated_text: Thus in the <s>Vājasaneyī</s>, this very one is the supreme consciousness.
Having first descended by her freedom into the knower whose form is breath,
flowing through the three channels whose nature is moon, sun, and fire,
entering and leaving within and without, marked by inhalation and exhalation,
drawing into herself time in its threefold form, past, present, and so on,

children.text: karṣanty antar bahiś ceti kathyate kālakarṣiṇī ||
children.translated_text: both within and without, she is called <s>Kālakarṣiṇī</s>, the drawer of time.
From this comes her natural connection with breath.
Even when the connection with breath remains, the one who has ascended to that,

children.text: saṃvidaṃ vimṛśann āste sa lokottaratāṃ vrajet ||
children.translated_text: and remains reflecting upon the inner consciousness, reaches a state beyond the world.
Thus <s>Maheśvara</s> speaks by way of summing up the means.
Of the dense channels extending to the openings of the eyes and other organs and to the pores of the hair,
among all those that are primary and that give support to everything,
in the paths of the left, right, and central channels, at all times,
the chief channel of the channels is the nasal one; the power of breath flows crookedly.

children.text: antar ity āntarī saṃvit tatsvarūpasya yat punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Inner' means the inner consciousness; and what again is the center of that one's own nature,
principal because it is the innermost of all and serving as the ground of the universe,
the form made of reflective awareness and transcendent, from restraint upon that,
from the excellence of intense beholding and from reflective awareness in the cognition of one's own self,

children.text: kim atra saṃyame vācyam iyam eva samāhitiḥ ||
children.translated_text: what more needs to be said here about restraint? This alone is concentration.
Blazing forth continuously within in all conditions,
it is experienced by the yogin through attention free from emergence from absorption.

children.text: mayy āveśya mano ye māṃ nityayuktā upāsate ||
children.translated_text: Those who, placing their mind in me, worship me, ever joined,

children.text: śraddhayā parayopetās te me yuktatamā matāḥ ||
children.translated_text: endowed with supreme faith, are considered by me the most deeply joined.
In accordance with the rule stated in the blessed <s>Bhagavadgītā</s>,
with his mind absorbed in his own I-ness that transcends the universe,
showing completely at the end the fruit of yoga for the yogin,
the glorious <s>Śiva</s> sums up the topic that has been stated.
And again, for the supreme yogin established in the highest yoga,
there would be the arising of the nature of consciousness that was previously stated.

children.text: bhūyaḥ syād iti vākyasya sphuṭam evāyam āśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This indeed is clearly the purport of the sentence 'there would again be.'

children.text: yac chivatvam amuṣyoktaṃ nāpūrvaṃ tat tu yoginaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The Śivatva that was said to belong to him is not something unprecedented for the yogin.
It is his very nature, raised up from himself by the power of that māyā.
Though shining of itself, because of the wickedness of conceptual construction this one

children.text: vimraṣṭuṃ kṣama ity asya proktopāyakrameṇa tat ||
children.translated_text: is not capable of reflecting upon it; through the sequence of means already stated,
that Śivatva becomes manifest. This auspicious teaching was spoken by <s>Śiva</s>.
Thus this is the third opening, indicating the <s>āṇavopāya</s> (atomic method).
Thus, of the revered <s>Śivasūtras</s>, expanded with their secret meaning,
there is another vārttika together with the portion of the vārttika stated before,
for those entitled to the crown-princeship of the kingdom of undivided consciousness.
For those whose wealth is the thirty-six tattvas, overpowered by the force of supreme valor,
for the princes of <s>Madhurāja</s>, who have mounted upon the great egoity,
by me, whose final birth has then been destroyed by the vision of the western one,
by <s>Varadarāja</s>, this dispeller of the delusion of māyā,
following the path of exposition determined by <s>Śrīkṣemarāja</s>,
has been made manifest directly and graciously by the worthy <s>Kṛṣṇadāsa</s>.
May the good people, having come to satisfaction, graciously accept this work.
